research_concepts: Opponent next-possession points per possession (PPP) conditional on preceding offensive play type
AVOID labels derived from defensive outcomes of play types
Own-sequence lag effects: team's own next-possession PPP after running a specific play type
Play-type classification reliability from play-by-play data
Cross-season stability of play-type effects on subsequent possessions
methodological_questions: Sample size and statistical power to detect between-play-type differences in opponent next-possession PPP
Confounding by game state (score margin, period, time remaining, opponent strength, lineup quality)
Multiple testing across many distinct play types
Measurement reliability of derived play-type labels from NBA play-by-play
Regression to the mean for play types with extreme observed next-possession PPP
Look-ahead bias when labeling plays retroactively based on future PPP outcomes
Sparsity of rare play types leading to unstable PPP estimates
Non-stationarity across seasons and offensive/defensive trends
evidence_does_not_establish: No prior studies retrieved for this specific question; the relationship between play type and opponent next-possession PPP, or own-sequence lag PPP, has not been previously assessed within this project's evidence base.
own_inferences: The data are sufficient in principle to compute opponent next-possession PPP and own next-possession PPP following each identified play type, using play-by-play and derived play-type possessions.

Common play types (pick-and-roll ball handler, isolation, post-up, spot-up, transition) have enough possessions across four seasons to allow detection of moderate effect sizes, but rare play types (e.g., off-screen, hand-off) likely lack power.
Large confounding is expected from game situation, opponent defensive quality, and lineup strength; without careful adjustment, apparent differences may be artifacts.
Multiple comparisons across dozens of play types require stringent correction, which will further reduce effective power for rarer types.
The own-sequence lag analysis adds a separate set of comparisons but is conceptually similar and faces the same methodological issues.

The AVOID label itself is an outcome-derived category; if it is defined solely by high opponent next-possession PPP from the same data, it is descriptive rather than predictive, and care must be taken not to overinterpret in-sample patterns.
uncertainties: Actual granularity and accuracy of play-type labels from the graph database is unknown; misclassification could dilute or bias estimates.
The operational definition of 'AVOID label'—threshold PPP, minimum sample size, and decision rule—is not specified in the question.
The extent to which next-possession outcomes are influenced by the preceding play type versus the many confounders cannot be known without analysis.
The temporal stability of effects across the 2022–2026 period is uncertain; rule changes or style trends may alter relationships.

historical_effect.explanation: No historical evidence was retrieved, so the decision rests solely on the assessment of data adequacy, testability, and methodological risks.

blocking_constraints.text: Rare play types (e.g., handoff, miscellaneous) may have fewer than 1000 opponent next-possessions, making PPP estimates too noisy to support reliable AVOID labels.
Game context (score, period, opponent, lineup) strongly influences next-possession outcomes; without identifying assumptions, separating the causal effect of play type is challenging.
Testing dozens of play types simultaneously inflates false positives; correction reduces power, especially for marginal effect sizes.

prior_work.summary: No earlier studies on this topic were available in the retrieval results. The question appears not to have been directly addressed in prior work by this project.

risks.text: Statistical power will be insufficient for infrequently used play types, leading to unreliable AVOID classifications based solely on observed PPP.
Opponent next-possession PPP is influenced by score differential, period, timeout usage, defensive matchups, and back-to-back schedules, all correlated with play-type selection.
Evaluating all play types for both opponent next-possession PPP and own-sequence PPP involves potentially >100 hypothesis tests, raising false discovery risk.
Play-type labels derived from play-by-play may misclassify possessions (e.g., transition vs. secondary break) introducing measurement error that attenuates or biases effect estimates.
Play types with low usage (e.g., alley-oop, post-up for non-centers) yield very few next-possession events within a season, making season-specific AVOID labels impossible.
If AVOID labels are defined using PPP outcomes from the very possessions used to measure the effect, the label is circular; future predictive validity would require out-of-sample testing.
Play types identified as extreme (best or worst) in one sample will tend to regress toward the mean in a subsequent sample, potentially invalidating AVOID labels.
Relationships may change across the four seasons due to coaching, rule changes, or offensive trends, complicating aggregation and interpretation.

design.estimand: For each distinct play type, the mean opponent points per possession on the opponent's immediately following possession, adjusted for game-state covariates; analogously, the mean team's own PPP on its next possession after running that play type.
design.unit: One possession: the next possession (by opponent, or by own team after regaining the ball) following a completed offensive possession with an identified play type. Exclude possessions following end-of-quarter/game and technical free throws.
design.sample: All regular-season and playoff games from NBA seasons 2022-23 through 2025-26 available as of 2026-06-19. Only play types with at least 500 occurrences in the pooled data are considered for AVOID labels; rarer types are reported descriptively.
design.power: For common play types (>10,000 occurrences), simulation-based power >80% to detect an opponent next-possession PPP difference of 0.03 (about 0.3 points per 10 possessions) at α=0.05 before multiplicity adjustment. For moderate types (2000–5000 occurrences), power to detect 0.05 PPP difference. Formal power simulation using historical PPP variance will be preregistered before analysis.
design.controls: Mixed-effects model with fixed effects for play type, and covariates: score margin (linear and quadratic), period (categorical), time remaining in quarter (restricted cubic spline), opponent defensive rating (season-long), possession start type (rebound, turnover, made basket, dead ball), home/away, rest days, and lineup strength (estimated via ridge regression on current players on court). Random intercepts for team, opponent, and season. Own-sequence models additionally control for whether the team retained possession on an offensive rebound.
design.falsification: 1. Placebo test: randomly permute the play-type labels among possessions and re-estimate; the distribution of effect sizes should be centered at zero. 2. Temporal stability: split the data into early/late seasons and test whether AVOID-flagged play types replicate. 3. Leave-one-season-out cross-validation of AVOID labels.
design.multiplicity: Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control at 10% across all play types tested for opponent next-possession PPP and own-sequence PPP separately. Bayesian hierarchical models will be used for shrinkage and posterior-based inference as a sensitivity analysis.
design.decision_rule: A play type qualifies for an AVOID label if (a) the adjusted opponent next-possession PPP is higher than the league-wide mean PPP with a one-sided false-discovery-rate-corrected p < 0.05 AND the estimated excess is at least 0.03 PPP; (b) the result replicates in a holdout season. Own-sequence lag effects are evaluated analogously: a play type is flagged as SELF-HURT if own next-possession PPP is significantly lower than average by at least 0.03 PPP. Joint AVOID+SELF-HURT types are highlighted for coaching consideration.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 per-game play-by-play data and derived play-type possession records as stored in the project's graph database, accessed on 2026-06-19. Exact data snapshots to be hashed and archived.

AVOID labels based on defensive outcomes
methodological_questions: sample size and power for detecting differences in opponent next-possession PPP by play type
confounding by game state, score, and period
look-ahead bias in labeling plays based on future outcomes
reliability of play-type classification from play-by-play

You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.

Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

We are in Stage 1. The task is to read the research question and data description, identify research concepts and methodological questions, then call retrieve_history. We must only output the retrieval call, no other text.

The research question: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter."

We need to parse this. It seems to be about evaluating opponent's points per possession on the next possession after a team runs a specific play type X. The claim is that this metric is large enough to drive "AVOID labels" (presumably labeling a play as one to avoid). Also, "own-sequence lags similarly matter" – likely meaning that the team's own subsequent possessions (maybe the next possession after running play X, or lags in the sequence) also matter.

We need to identify research concepts and methodological questions. Research concepts: opponent next-possession PPP, play type labeling, AVOID labels, own-sequence lags. Methodological questions: sample size, reliability, confounding, look-ahead bias, etc. We'll formulate these for the retrieval.

The data available: NBA seasons 2022-23 through 2025-26 (partial). Play-by-play data, substitutions, defensive matchups, derived play-type possession records. So it's rich.

Now, we need to retrieve_history with these arguments. The function signature: retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query). All are lists or strings? It expects lists for research_concepts and methodological_questions, and a string for query. We'll craft these.

Research concepts: 
- "opponent next-possession points per possession (PPP) after specific play types"
- "AVOID labels based on defensive outcomes"
- "own-sequence lags in play-type effectiveness"
- "play-type labeling and data quality"
- "play-type possession records"

Methodological questions: 
- "sample size and power for detecting differences in opponent next-possession PPP by play type"
- "confounding by game state, score, and period"
- "look-ahead bias in labeling plays based on future outcomes"
- "reliability of play-type classification from play-by-play"
- "regression to the mean in extreme play-type outcomes"
- "multiple testing across many play types"

Query: a concise sentence describing the research question. "Investigate whether opponent next-possession PPP after running a specific play type is large enough to justify AVOID labels, and whether own-sequence lags similarly matter for play type evaluation."

Now, we output the JSON with action tool, tool retrieve_history, args. Only that, no other text.

We are in stage 2 now. We got zero historical results. So no prior studies to cite. We need to provide the full output.

We need to carefully consider the research question: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter."

Interpretation: The researcher wants to see if, after running a specific play type X, the opponent's next possession PPP (points per possession) is significantly different/higher (or lower? presumably AVOID labels are for plays that lead to good opponent outcomes), and if that effect is large enough to justify labeling that play type as AVOID (i.e., a play that increases opponent scoring, so you should avoid it). Additionally, "own-sequence lags similarly matter": they want to know if the PPP on your own next possession after running play X (or own sequence of possessions) also matters similarly. So basically evaluating play types not just by immediate outcome but by subsequent possession outcomes for both teams.

Data: NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 seasons, per-game play-by-play data, substitution rotations, defensive matchups, derived play-type possession records in a graph database (initiator, play type, points). So they have labeled possessions by play type (likely based on some algorithm). They want to compute opponent next-possession PPP and own next-possession PPP by play type.

Potential issues: sample size per play type, especially if many play types; look-ahead bias (using future PPP to label plays? That seems weird but the AVOID label would be derived from the outcome, so data leakage if used for prediction? Actually they want to see if opponent next-possession PPP is large enough to drive AVOID labels—i.e., to determine that a play type is "bad" defensively. But defining AVOID based on observed PPP could be tautological. They might be asking: if we compute opponent next-possession PPP after each play type, is the range large enough to meaningfully categorize some play types as AVOID? That is testable without leakage if we just compute PPP and see if there's statistically significant variation and large effect sizes. But risk: multiple testing across many play types; small sample sizes for rare play types; confounding by game state (score, time, opponent quality, lineup). Opponent next possession PPP depends on many factors, not just the preceding offensive play type. The play type might be correlated with game situation (e.g., isolation plays in clutch, transition plays off turnovers). Own-sequence lags: consecutive possessions from same team, but also influenced by momentum, opponent adjustments.

Methodological risks: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (many play types, small samples), CONFOUNDING (game situation, opponent, lineup, home/away, etc.), MULTIPLE_TESTING (testing many play types), MEASURE_RELIABILITY (play type classification accuracy from play-by-play may be noisy, especially distinguishing play types like pick-and-roll vs handoff, etc.), LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD? Not directly unless they use future data to define AVOID, but they are just labeling retrospectically based on PPP, not using it for prediction, so maybe not. However, if they use PPP from the same games to both select AVOID plays and evaluate them, there's overfitting. RTM_SELECTION: extreme play types may regress to mean in subsequent games. DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY across seasons. EXPOSURE_SPARSITY: rare play types will have few opponent possessions, leading to high variance. OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL: if AVOID is based on PPP itself, that's circular but they may be asking if PPP differences are large enough to justify the label. That's not a bias if it's just a description. BASE_RATE: opponent PPP may have high baseline variance.

Testability: I think it's testable with the data, but power might be low for rare play types. They have multiple seasons, so potentially enough data for common play types. The question is whether the effect sizes (difference in opponent next-possession PPP) between play types are "large enough to drive AVOID labels" — that's subjective but they can measure the variance and magnitude.

Given no prior evidence, we proceed with a design.

I need to assign probabilities to predicted_outcome: supported, rejected, untestable, artifact, uncertain. Given the data and risks, I'd guess it could be supported if there are systematic differences (like transition plays vs. half-court sets leading to different opponent subsequent possessions). But many play types may show no difference. I'd put some probability on uncertain due to confounding. I'll assign: supported 0.3, rejected 0.2, untestable 0.1, artifact 0.05, uncertain 0.35. But these are just guesses.

Decision: proceed_with_changes? The question as posed is: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter." It's not a precise hypothesis but a broad research question. Need to narrow down: specific play types, define AVOID label criteria, control for confounders. Probably proceed_with_changes, specifying that we need precise definitions and a plan to address confounding and multiple testing.

Design: Estimand: average opponent next-possession PPP and own next-possession PPP for each play type, controlling for game context. Unit: a possession (either opponent next possession following a play of type X). Sample: all possessions from NBA regular season and playoff games from listed seasons where play type can be identified and next possession is not end-of-quarter/game. Power: I'd need to do simulations, but with thousands of possessions per common play type, effect sizes of 0.05 PPP (which is meaningful) might be detectable. Controls: score differential, period, time remaining, opponent defensive rating, lineup strength, home/away, rest days, and previous possession outcome. Falsification: test if results are robust across seasons, split-half, and using placebos (e.g., randomizing next possession assignment). Multiplicity: use false discovery rate control for many play types. Decision rule: declare a play type as AVOID candidate if its adjusted opponent next-possession PPP is significantly higher than the league average with effect size ≥ 0.03 PPP after multiple comparisons correction, and also check own-sequence PPP.

Historical effect: no historical evidence, so no change.

Now we need to produce the JSON. It must be a final action with output object.

Check all required fields. Use risk codes: appropriate ones: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, CONFOUNDING, MULTIPLE_TESTING, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, maybe RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL? Not really derived label unless they use same data to both define AVOID and test, but they just want to see if differences exist. So less likely.

I'll craft design details.

Data version: "NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 seasons as available on 2026-06-19, per-game play-by-play and derived play-type possession records."

Power: "Power analysis to be conducted via simulation; with ~2460 games per regular season and 4 seasons, common play types (isolation, pick-and-roll ball handler, post-up, spot-up) each have >10,000 possessions, giving >80% power to detect a difference of 0.03 PPP at α=0.05 before multiple testing correction; rarer play types may be underpowered."

Decision rule: "After controlling for covariates, compute Bayesian hierarchical estimates of opponent next-possession PPP per play type. Flag a play type as 'AVOID' if the posterior probability that its PPP exceeds the population mean by ≥0.03 is >0.95, and also check own-sequence lag effects."

I need to ensure all output.

I'll write the final JSON.
